sample.title: Al Asr - A Civilization in Loss
sample.author: Noor Library
sample.description:
The journey through Surah Al-'Asr began with a stark oath: وَالْعَصْرِ (By Time), and concluded with the four pillars of salvation.

We have diagnosed the condition of modern humanity - a civilization in loss, overwhelmed by distraction and consumption, losing time while believing it is gaining speed. The cure remains constant: إِلَّا الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا وَعَمِلُوا الصَّالِحَاتِ وَتَوَاصَوْا بِالْحَقِّ وَتَوَاصَوْا بِالصَّبْرِ.

True success is found not in accumulation, but in alignment - through faith, righteous action, truth, and patience. May this reflection serve as a permanent check against the current of heedlessness. The time for transformation is now.

sample.title: Signs Beyond the Visible
sample.author: Author Al-Noor
sample.description:
This series explores some of the most profound signs mentioned in the Qur'an. It is not a scientific textbook, nor a traditional commentary. Rather, it is a journey of reflection. 

We will look at the signs Allah presented to awaken hearts, strengthen certainty, and remind humanity of realities beyond what is immediately visible.

episodes.title: The Ruined City
episodes.plainTextContent:
Allah says:
﴿ أَوْ كَالَّذِي مَرَّ عَلَىٰ قَرْيَةٍ وَهِيَ خَاوِيَةٌ عَلَىٰ عُرُوشِهَا ۖ قَالَ أَنَّىٰ يُحْيِي هَٰذِهِ اللَّهُ بَعْدَ مَوْتِهَا ﴾
"Or like the one who passed by a town which had collapsed upon its roofs. He said: How will Allah bring this to life after its death?" (Al-Baqarah 2:259)
The Qur'an often introduces its greatest lessons in the simplest ways. No name is mentioned. No lengthy background is provided. We are simply presented with a traveler, a ruined town, and a question. Yet within this scene lies a sign powerful enough to awaken the heart, humble the intellect, and strengthen certainty in Allah.
The man was passing by a town that had once been alive. Families had lived there. Children had played in its streets. Markets had once been filled with movement and conversation. Life had flourished within its walls. Now all that remained were ruins.


The Qur'an describes it as:
﴿ وَهِيَ خَاوِيَةٌ عَلَىٰ عُرُوشِهَا ﴾
"Collapsed upon its roofs."
Its buildings had fallen upon themselves. The structures remained, but their purpose had vanished. What was once full of life now stood as a monument to absence.
Perhaps one of the reasons Allah repeatedly directs our attention to the remains of past peoples is because ruins expose a truth that prosperity often conceals. When societies are strong, they imagine themselves permanent. When wealth increases, people begin to feel secure. When civilizations dominate, they rarely imagine their own decline.
Yet every ruin on earth tells the same story: nothing created is permanent.
The ancient Egyptians believed their civilization would endure forever. The Romans ruled vast portions of the known world. Powerful kingdoms rose across Asia, Africa, Europe, and the Americas. They built monuments, armies, roads, palaces, and cities. Many assumed their greatness would never fade.


Today, most survive only in books, museums, archaeological sites, and scattered memories.
Time reduced certainty into history.
This is one of the first signs hidden within the story. Before Allah demonstrates resurrection, He first presents destruction. Before He shows life, He shows death. Before He displays restoration, He presents collapse.
The ruined city is not merely the setting of the story. It is the first lesson of the story.
Modern man is not very different from those who came before him. We have more technology, more information, and more comfort than many previous generations, but we suffer from the same illusion. We assume our achievements make us secure.
We trust institutions, economies, governments, technology, and progress. Yet history repeatedly demonstrates that civilizations do not collapse because they expect to collapse. Most decline while believing they are stronger than ever.
The Qur'an constantly calls humanity to study what came before.
﴿ قُلْ سِيرُوا فِي الْأَرْضِ فَانظُرُوا كَيْفَ كَانَ عَاقِبَةُ الَّذِينَ مِن قَبْلُ ﴾
"Say: Travel through the earth and observe how was the end of those before."


The believer is not meant to look at history merely as information. He is meant to look at it as a warning.
The remains of destroyed nations are among Allah's signs. They testify that strength without gratitude eventually weakens, power without justice eventually corrupts, and civilizations without moral foundations eventually decline.
Every fallen nation whispers the same message to those willing to listen:
"Do not be deceived as we were deceived."
Standing before the ruins, the traveler asks:
﴿ أَنَّىٰ يُحْيِي هَٰذِهِ اللَّهُ بَعْدَ مَوْتِهَا ﴾
"How will Allah bring this to life after its death?"
This question marks the beginning of our journey.


Notice that his attention is drawn not to how the city was destroyed, but how it could ever live again. Destruction seemed understandable. Restoration seemed impossible.
This is often the limitation of human perception. We understand what we can observe repeatedly. We see buildings constructed and buildings demolished. We witness growth and decay. But resurrection belongs to a reality beyond ordinary human experience.
The man was not denying Allah's power. Rather, he was standing before a reality so overwhelming that he sought understanding.
Many people today ask similar questions, even if they phrase them differently.
How can the dead be raised?
How can bones return to life?
How can something that has completely decayed be restored?
How can a world filled with death witness resurrection again?
These questions are not new. Humanity has asked them throughout history. Yet the Qur'an consistently directs people toward the signs already surrounding them.
The seed that disappears beneath the soil and emerges as a living plant.
The barren earth that becomes green after rainfall.
The child brought forth from a tiny drop.
The daily cycle of sleep and awakening.
Creation itself is a continuous reminder that Allah brings life from what appears lifeless.
Before the miracle unfolds, the ruined city leaves us with a reflection.


Everything around us is moving toward one of two destinations: preservation by the will of Allah or decay by the will of Allah.
Our bodies age.
Our homes deteriorate.
Our possessions wear out.
Entire societies rise and fall.
Generations appear and disappear.
Yet mankind continues to live as though permanence belongs to him.
We plan for decades while forgetting eternity.
We build as though we will remain forever.
We pursue status as though death cannot reach us.
The ruins stand as a correction to this illusion.
The silence of the ruined city speaks louder than many words.
Its broken walls testify that power fades.
Its empty streets testify that life is temporary.
Its collapse testifies that every worldly achievement eventually meets its limit.
And perhaps that is why Allah begins this story with ruins.
For before man can understand resurrection, he must first understand mortality.
Before he can appreciate life, he must confront death.
Before he can witness restoration, he must acknowledge destruction.
And before Allah shows him the miracle of resurrection, He first teaches him one of the greatest signs of all:
Everything that is not Allah is passing away.
﴿ كُلُّ مَنْ عَلَيْهَا فَانٍ ۝ وَيَبْقَىٰ وَجْهُ رَبِّكَ ذُو الْجَلَالِ وَالْإِكْرَامِ ﴾
"Everyone upon it will perish. And there will remain the Face of your Lord, Owner of Majesty and Honor." (Ar-Rahman 55:26-27)
The story has only just begun. Yet the ruins have already delivered their lesson.
The question now is not what happened to the city.
The question is whether we are paying attention to the signs hidden within its ruins.
